# APPROVAL.

BY order of My Lord the Chancellor, I have read a manuscript bearing the title *The History of the Heavens, Considered according to the Ideas of the Poets, the Philosophers, and of Moses, etc.* By Monsieur <note>original: "den Heer." This refers to Abbé Noël-Antoine Pluche (1688–1761), a French priest whose works on natural history and mythology were immensely popular.</note> PLUCHE. One cannot sufficiently praise the Author, who has directed his entire purpose toward Religion and good morals. The public has already applauded the first works <note>A reference to Pluche's "Le Spectacle de la nature," a massive multi-volume work on natural history that became a bestseller in the 18th century.</note> to come from the same hand; and I do not doubt in any way that it will also receive this work favorably; which presents a New System <note>original: "Sistema." In the 18th century, "System" often referred to a comprehensive theoretical framework used to explain a complex subject.</note> regarding Fable-lore (Mythology), regarding the entire Pagan Religion, and regarding the use of Reason, and urges it with great Learning.

->In Paris, the 6th of June, 1738.<-

# Explanation of the Plates.

Page 322. 1. *Horus* swaddled and carrying the Measuring-rod with the hoopoe's head, the square, and the trumpet; all of which are announcements of the subsiding of the waters, and of the subsequent surveying of the Lands. <note>In this context, Horus is depicted as a mummy, symbolizing the seeds "buried" or dormant during the Nile's flood. The measuring rod and square refer to the ancient practice of re-surveying agricultural land boundaries after the floodwaters receded and deposited new silt.</note> <note>original: "hoppen hooft." The hoopoe bird was a common symbol in Egyptian iconography; here it crowns the measuring rod used for land surveying.</note>

2. *The Harpy*, or the New Moon which is accompanied by the return of destructive pests. <note>While typically seen as monsters in Greek mythology, the author interprets the Harpy here as a celestial messenger marking the arrival of vermin during certain lunar phases.</note>

3. *The Graces* or the three beauties. <note>original: "De Charites." In Greek mythology, these are the goddesses of charm, beauty, and fertility.</note>

Page 338. 1. *The Fate* or *Goddess of Destiny*; or the announcement of weaving. <note>original: "De Park of Schikgodin." The "Parcae" or Fates were believed to spin, measure, and cut the thread of human life; here, the author links them to the actual industry of weaving.</note>

2. *The Siren*, or the Announcement of the Months of the flood and of rest. <note>The author likely associates the Siren's song with the period of the Nile's inundation when agricultural labor ceased and the land lay "at rest" under water.</note>

3. *The Eumenide*, or a fury; the announcement of the pressing of grapes, olives, and apples. <note>The "Eumenides" or Furies are repurposed here as seasonal markers for the harvest and the mechanical labor of the presses.</note>

4. *The Snakes*, Emblems of the maintenance of life. <note>original: "Zinnebeelden van 's Leevens-onderhoudt." Because snakes shed their skins, they were ancient symbols of regeneration and the cyclical renewal of the food supply.</note>

See how Democritus has withdrawn into his native lands
And into the tombs of Abdera,
Where he, undistracted and freed from the bustle,
Has the contemplation of the world’s structure as his
   goal,
Which he firmly believes was born from the convergence
Of particles, previously [held to be] indivisible*.
   See here with the Philosopher a citizen from the city,
With a slate <note>original: "Schalie"</note> that contains this verse in Greek:
*Man was not made to fashion the Earth,*
*But, by cultivating it, to sustain himself. †*
See the farm laborers <note>original: "Akkerlien"</note> and those who pass by all day,
Mocking the Philosopher with their gestures and laughter.
Each of them believes that all men
Received as much [knowledge] as they could reasonably wish for;
Since their knowledge clearly enough reveals to them
The rule that serves the benefit of their morals,
And of their labor; while they regard all the rest—
Yet do not understand that which the Gods do not entrust
To their care—whereby their knowledge is halted
And their understanding limited. This is the aim of this
   Work.

The history of this confusion must therefore necessarily contain two very distinct subjects: namely, the first institution of the names and images that were, in the course of time, honored as Gods; and in the second place, the misconception through which one attributed <term>Divinity</term> <note>original: "Godheidt"</note> and religious honor to them. The other part truly makes human Reason <note>original: "Reede"</note> feel entirely ashamed; however, it is of great concern to us, whether for the removal of many common folk-delusions, or because it clearly shows us that the human spirit—when governed by immoderate desire and when it abandons the simplicity of <term>revelation</term> <note>original: "oopenbaring," referring to divine truth revealed to man</note> or neglects its wholesome teachings—must necessarily go astray.

# FIRST CHAPTER.

## CONCERNING THE ORIGIN OF THE NAMES WHICH THE ANCIENTS GAVE TO THE VARIOUS PARTS OF THE HEAVENS.

<margin>
GENERAL CUSTOMS.
</margin>
One cannot form a sound judgment regarding the origin of the names that Antiquity <note>original: "Outheidt"</note> gave to the various parts of the Heaven and to the whole of Nature, except insofar as one knows what ideas occupied their minds and what their primary interests were. But where, indeed, shall we find the thoughts and inclinations of the first Men, if not in the monuments <note>original: "gedenkteekenen," referring to historical records, ruins, or physical artifacts</note> that have come down to us from them? Let us then immediately proceed to the investigation of their customs and these memorials, in order to derive from them the truth and those principles or origins that we wish to understand.

## I.

### Origin of the customs common to all Nations.

<margin>ORIGIN OF THE POETIC HEAVEN.</margin>
WE sometimes marvel at the similarity found in certain matters between the customs of God’s People <note>The author refers to the Israelites or Hebrews as "God's People."</note> and those of the Nations who were surrendered to the grossest Idolatry <note>original: "Afgodendienft," referring to the worship of physical idols or false gods.</note>.

It was customary among the Hebrews, as among all other Peoples, to assemble in a place chosen and set apart for that purpose to praise God; to offer Him Bread, Salt, the Fruits of the Earth, and the usual first-fruits <note>original: "eerfstelingen," the first portion of a harvest traditionally dedicated to a deity.</note> of the necessities of life, or to bring Him public thanksgivings for them; to offer Sacrifices; to eat in common that which had been offered to the Lord; and to add to the thanksgiving the singing and the sound of Musical Instruments.

It was also a general custom, both among the Hebrews and among all Nations, to bury the dead, to treat them with reverence, and to gather at their Burial-places <note>original: "Begraafplaatſen"</note> on certain days to praise God there.

...nothing was more necessary; nothing could have been better devised.

While humanity multiplied exceedingly, the labor and life of men could not be properly managed and regulated except through an accurate knowledge of the course of the sun <note>original: "Zonnen-Loop"</note>, and by the convenience of announcing its various movements. To this end, the constellations <note>original: "gesterntens"</note>, among which the sun was seen to go and return, were divided into twelve equal parts;
<margin>
*See Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book I, Chapter 21. Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*. *Spectacle of Nature*, Volume 4, Part 2, Discourse I.
</margin>
*because it had been noted that the sun passed through them once in the time that the moon made its circuit about or slightly more than twelve times. And thus all the deeds and occupations that were to keep human society busy throughout the course of an entire year were expressed with twelve words. If, therefore, the use of these twelve words, and of the twelve parts of the year that correspond with them, has passed to most nations, then this is a new proof that this usage, and even these names, have emerged from the common origin of the human race <note>original: "Menschelyken geslachts"</note>.

# IV.

## *Invention of Picture-Writing.*

The twelve symbolic names that represented the twelve parts of both the year and the Heavens were of great assistance in regulating the start of the sowing-time <note>original: "Zaeitydt"</note>, haying-time <note>original: "hooy-tydt"</note>, harvest-time <note>original: "Maeitydt"</note>, the general hunting seasons, and the other activities of social life.

<margin>The ZODIAC.</margin>
They presented to the mind twelve objects whose likenesses are very recognizable; and to make their use more convenient, they were represented in rough outlines on shells or on stones. It was essentially nothing more than an imperfect depiction outlined only with strokes; but since the sketching <note>original: "afschetsing"</note> of a painting is its very beginning, it is probable that the art of painting <note>original: "Schilderkunst"</note> owes its birth to the rough sketches of the twelve celestial signs <note>original: "Heemelteekenen"</note>. Yet the reader can very easily perceive that such depictions, publicly displayed to announce a certain specific kind of activity or work—or even two or three of those likenesses joined together near one another to indicate a certain number of months—intended to express something entirely different to the mind...

<margin>Signs and causes of the flooding.</margin>
From year to year they experienced that the flooding was always preceded by a steady annual wind (the Etesian) (*a*), which, around the time the sun passes through the constellation of **Cancer**, blowing from the North to the South, drove the vapors southward; and collected these in the interior (*b*) of the land, from where the Nile has its source; and caused abundant rains there; made the water of the river swell; and subsequently brought the flooding into all of Egypt, without the inhabitants noticing the slightest rain there.

It may well be that they did not understand the chain of these effects in the way we now present them; however, without reasoning uselessly about the causes and the outcome, they did notice that the North wind was always followed by the flood; and that the flood was violent or weak according to the strength and duration of that wind, which was not exactly equal every year.

This Wind, which had now become an infallible sign of the rising of the waters...

### VIII.

### *Interpretation of the Egyptian Emblems.*

If we wish to interpret some of the most common Egyptian emblems in a proper manner, one must not, in my opinion, seek their explanation in the ideas of the divine Plato; nor in the teachings that Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher who often sought deep allegorical meanings in ancient myths.</note> and Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians," interpreting their rituals through a mystical lens.</note> have written about guardian spirits (*genii*), nor in the metaphysics of any modern philosopher. Let us instead consult the practical needs of the Egyptian colony: It is there that one must naturally seek the meaning of the depictions that were displayed before the eyes of the entire assembly of the people.

It was not enough for the priests, or the public officials, to carefully observe the exact measure of the rising water; the people also had to be informed of it. It is probable that, to provide for this, three or four types of vases, or measures, were erected in public. These, being of unequal capacity—though well known to the people—served to indicate the three or four different heights caused by the varying rise of the Nile, without the need for criers or messengers. There are two things that convince me that the meaning of these vases, or wide-bellied measures—so common in Egyptian monuments—relates to this purpose. The first is the name attributed to them; the second is the additions that accompany them. 

Regarding the first: the name *Canob* or *Canopus* <note>original: "Canob" or "Canope." Commonly one finds the <term>Canopic Vases</term> <note>original: "Canopen." While today these are known as funerary jars, the author treats them here as symbolic vessels used by the Egyptians to represent the Nile.</note>, with one or two crosses at the end, the meaning of which we have already explained. Very often one also finds various bird heads atop the upper part of the Vase, acting as signs for the various winds known to them; these winds either assisted or obstructed the rising or the receding of the waters. Sometimes they placed a dog’s head upon the Canopus to signify the state of the River at the time of the appearance of the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, whose appearance in the dawn sky signaled the annual flooding of the Nile.</note>. At another time, they placed a maiden’s head upon it to represent the state of the Nile under the sign of <term>Virgo</term> <note>original: "de Maagdt," the Virgin. This refers to the sun's position in the zodiac during the late summer.</note>, and the approaching time of the drying of the lands.

When one unites all these conjectures together, they seem to constitute a complete certainty; and the greater the correspondence they had to the primary needs of that <term>colony</term> <note>original: "Volkplanting." The author views ancient Egyptian society as a foundational settlement or civilization organized around the Nile’s cycles.</note>, the more acceptable they become. Let us then follow this attempt at explanation, since it already begins to shed some faint light over a subject that until now was very obscure, and the knowledge of which would untangle many <term>Monuments of Antiquity</term> <note>original: "Gedenkteekenen der Oudtheidt."</note>.

<margin>THE SYMBOLIC WRITING</margin>
Whoever may have been the inventor of the first Symbols, which were particularly unique to Egypt, is of no concern to us, nor can it contribute anything to their clarification; it is enough to know that they were received everywhere with acclaim. The ease of this language, which made itself understood at a glance, and which made the animals and even the stones speak the same language, gradually made its use more common; they were, therefore, used for all things.

Very soon the <term>Hieroglyphic writing</term> <note>original: "Beeldenschrift," literally "image-writing." The author is describing the transition from symbolic objects to a formal system of pictograms.</note> served as much for the instruction of Morals as for the management of Agriculture; it was used to preserve the knowledge of the most important truths among the People and to instill in them their primary duties. ### X.

### *The Symbols of the Year. The Solar Year. Osiris.*

Since the whole of Egyptian society had the utmost need to determine the order of their days and to reach agreement with one another regarding the times when they should gather together, rest, or undertake collective labor, nothing more useful could be invented for this purpose than Pictographic Writing <note>original: "Beeldenfchrift"; an early term for hieroglyphs or symbolic imagery used to convey meaning before the decipherment of the Rosetta Stone</note>. This was because it was very easy, through certain signs displayed in public, to announce the festivals and the times of specific occupations in a simple and uniform manner.

The course of the Year relates to three main subjects: 1. the path of the Sun; 2. the order of the Festivals for each season; 3. general occupations. We shall begin with the Symbols of the Sun.

One could, with sufficient justification, call the arrangement of the feasts here the *Ecclesiastical Year*; since those feasts were religious gatherings where people made it their work to honor God and to glorify Him for His providence. For the investigation we have at hand regarding the original customs and the meaning of the ancient script <note>The author refers here to "Ancient Scripture" or symbolic writing, likely hieroglyphs or proto-alphabetic symbols used before the rise of formalized paganism.</note> looks entirely at the times that preceded the introduction of Idolatry. New Moon signified; that the Full Moon, placed on the head or on the breast of *Isis*, signified the feast that was to be held in the middle of the month; that the Crescent <note>original: "Wassende", literally waxing</note> or the Full Moon, accompanied by these or those leaves, announced the gathering that was to be held on a Full or New Moon occurring closest to this or that harvest; that a radiant star, placed in her headdress, was a herald of an offering to be performed in the morning at the rising of the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, whose rising coincided with the flooding of the Nile</note>; or of some other planet, and in such other circumstances as might be useful for distinguishing the feasts or the seasons. All these changes each had a particular meaning; and thus *Isis* changed her garments, just as the Earth does.

When the priests—alongside *Isis*, who wore a crescent moon on her head and carried a sickle in her hand—displayed an *Osiris* with his bushel or grain measure <note>original: "Scheepel", a traditional unit of dry volume</note> to the assembly of the people, the people could easily understand that there was a solemn offering and an annual distribution to be held on that New Moon which occurs just before the harvest. A single example of this symbolic language is enough to make one understand how easily the meaning, as well as the placements and additions, could be understood—

# XII.

## Rural Labor, or the Agricultural Year.

->Horus<-

The first Egyptian teachers seem to have concerned themselves little with precise observations and speculations in their teachings. Their great aim was to instill feelings of gratitude toward God into the People, and to regulate their labor, upon whose successful outcome their lives depended. A Philosopher, who is filled with some system of physics, or with lofty ideas about the Nature of Spirits, will immediately, upon seeing the hieroglyphic writing <note>original: "Beeldenſchrift", literally image-script</note> of the Egyptians, seek his beloved thesis therein, and believe he can well perceive it there.

But let us harbor neither prejudices nor systems, for those are essentially the same thing. When one knows the human heart, one can easily deduce the purpose of its actions from its needs; and so it is that from the investigation of the needs of the Egyptian colony, one can discover the lessons of Thoth <note>The Egyptian god of wisdom, writing, and magic, credited with inventing the alphabet</note> and the meaning of the principal characters of [the script] in a reasonable and probable manner.

### XIV.
### *Horus, or the Symbols of the various Annual Labors.*

These representations of Horus, passing from one nation to another, have undoubtedly become more or less varied according to the whims or imaginations of those who adopted these ceremonies as their own; they gave rise, at the same time, to a multitude of tales and fables. However, their meaning in its first origin was simple and clear; and this is what we are tracing here. The truth of the explanation we gave for the representation of Horus can be justified by the account of the various forms he was made to assume, since they all serve to demonstrate some of the annual results of agriculture, or the obstacles that one encountered...

Now that we have learned the letters of the Egyptian script <note>Hieroglyphics or symbolic writing.</note> with regard to agriculture <term>Akkerbouw (the cultivation of fields)</term>, let us set ourselves to the writing. Let us conduct an experiment to draw in the Egyptian manner. In order to enclose many things in a small space, let us make use of the privilege to unite, within a single body, various abstract parts of several different images. The binding together of these pieces will be able to signify just as much as if we saw them all in their entirety. The abbreviation of these forms will be easy; and although these combinations are not actually found in nature, their very strangeness will make the people all the more attentive regarding the meaning <term>Zin (the hidden sense or symbolic logic)</term> that is hidden therein.

On his head he bore the natural signs of a happy Harvest; namely two jars (a) with Wine or Beer, upon which three loaves of bread lay; accompanied by leaves, herbs, and various Fruits. Sometimes his knees seemed to bend under the heavy burden. Often he was depicted sitting, to signify the rest of which he ensured the enjoyment for Men. He held his Finger to his Mouth (b), and thereby exhorted the bystanders—by no means to the secret of mysteries, which is a notion of later times when the meaning of the Images was entirely lost or changed—but to temperance <note>original: 'maetigheidt'</note>; submission to the Laws; modesty, and prudence <note>original: 'bedachtfaemheidt'</note>; in a word, to Peace, without which Man must necessarily lose the possession of the Fruits obtained through his labor.

But he has convinced me of nothing, except for his own erudition. The true meaning of this, our symbol <note>original: 'Zinnebeeldt'</note>, and the instruction this writing gave to the People was: *Peace and civil order among the Citizens, after the harvests, and in the joy inspired by the rest of Winter.*

We find the proof for this in the combination of three circumstances, which remove all doubt and ambiguity on the matter. The first is the bearing of the Fruits with which Horus is laden; the second is the name given to him when he is shown in that state; the third consists of the gestures or posture of that figure. The bread, the Wine, the Fruits, legumes, hay, or large dried crops with which his head is decorated, rest directly upon the two large horns of a Capricorn <note>The zodiac sign Capricorn, which the sun enters at the winter solstice.</note>; and thus it was almost impossible to indicate the complete abundance that the Farmer <note>original: 'Landtman'</note> enjoys at the beginning of Winter, when the Sun enters Capricorn, in a simpler way or with fewer hidden mysteries. If the posture of the Finger on the mouth of Harpocrates has deceived Ancient and modern interpreters, it is because they have judged the meaning of that image based on that posture alone; whereas they should have judged the Meaning of the posture based on the accompanying attributes and the functions expressed in the meaning of his Name. Angerona, whom the Romans held to be the Goddess of silence because she held her finger to her lips, was in her origin nothing other than an imitation of the Egyptian Harpocrates <note>Harpocrates was the Greek adaptation of the Egyptian child-god Horus, often depicted with a finger to his mouth, which Greeks and Romans misinterpreted as a gesture of silence.</note> and an invitation to peace in the midst of the winter's rest. ## XVII.

### *Continuation of the Memorials of the Past.*

<margin>
SYMBOLIC
CEREMONIES.
</margin>
We have already noted that the ancients were not satisfied with expressing certain truths solely by means of depictions on stones. They also utilized theatrical ceremonies <note>original: *Toneelplechtigheden*; ritualized performances or pageants where history was reenacted through costume and movement</note> in which both the objects and the names of the performers held allegorical <note>original: *Zinspeelende*; referring to a deeper, symbolic meaning beyond the literal action</note> significance. These were useful for keeping the memory of past events alive in the mind.

The festival commemorating the ancient state of the Human Race after the Great Flood <note>original: *Zondvloedt*; referring to the biblical Deluge of Noah</note> appears to have begun even before the dispersion <note>A reference to the "Dispersion of Nations" following the Tower of Babel, according to biblical chronology</note>. However, it took on a grander form in Egypt through the use of symbolic figures, which were far more numerous there than elsewhere. This festival, having become common to all nations, deserves a more thorough explanation than what has already been said of it. We cannot explain its symbols without simultaneously shedding a great and useful light upon the vast multitude of monuments <term>Gedenkteekens: literally "memory-signs," referring to physical remains, inscriptions, or ruins from antiquity</term> that remain to us, and which until now have been considered unintelligible.

### XVIII.

## *Living Animals become Symbolic.*

<margin>THE POETIC HEAVEN.</margin>
Now that we are familiar with the taste the Eastern peoples, and especially the Egyptians, had for symbolic figures, we have the right to believe that the particular customs observed among them were so many signs of certain truths, whether astronomical, moral, or otherwise. We may then now safely say that the Ram, which was honored in Thebes and in Libya; the Bull honored at Memphis and Heliopolis; the Goats honored at Mendes; the Lion, the Fish, and other animals to which honor was paid in various regions, were in their origin very simple symbols <term>original: Zinnebeelden; emblems intended to convey a deeper meaning</term>. They were nothing other than the ancient signs of the Zodiac <term>original: Dier-kring; literally "animal-circle"</term> and the various markers of the solstices <note>The author is suggesting that animal worship did not start as religion, but as a calendar system to track the sun's position through the year.</note>. The inhabitants of Mendes <note>Mendes was an ancient Egyptian city in the Nile Delta, famous for its cult of the ram (often referred to as a goat in historical texts).</note> honored the Goats and ate the Sheep; those of Thebes <note>Thebes was the capital of Upper Egypt; its patron deity, Amun, was often depicted as a ram, leading to the local veneration of sheep.</note>, on the contrary, honored the Sheep and ate the Goats. And thus one can suspect, along with most scholars, that the utility and profit of commerce were the motivations that made the Egyptians love these animals, and which made the sight of them so pleasant in their festivals.

However, as likely as this conjecture regarding the origin of the honoring of animals in Egypt might be, here is something more certain regarding this strange custom—about which so much has been written without the true origin having been indicated. Monsieur Maillet <note>Benoît de Maillet (1656–1738) was a French diplomat and natural historian who served as the consul in Cairo. His writings provided Europeans with some of the most detailed accounts of Egypt at the time.</note>, in his description of Egypt, which he knew very well after a sixteen-year stay there, teaches us that in Lower Egypt the harvest occurs in the month of May; above Cairo in April; and in Upper Egypt in March or even earlier.

Since the harvest was the object that most powerfully moved the spirit of the people, the New Moon <note>The lunar calendar was central to Egyptian religious life, with each new moon marking the start of a new month and often a specific seasonal festival.</note> that concluded the gathering of the crops necessarily had to be one of the most pleasant of all their festivals.

I shall conclude the history of Egyptian script, and the examples of meaningful or instructional customs, with a brief account concerning the ceremonies for the deceased and their significance.

Near every city of Egypt, there was a sacred place serving as its general burial ground. Diodorus the Sicilian <note>Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE; his works are a primary source for modern understanding of ancient Egyptian customs.</note> informs us how these graveyards were arranged and what was performed there, providing a precise description of the general burial ground of Memphis, which was the largest and most visited of all. This general burial ground, according to his account, was situated across a lake named *Acherusia* <note>original: *Acherusi*</note>. On the shore of that lake <note>Likely Lake Moeris, which served as a central site for these funeral rituals.</note>, there was a strict ferryman who could not be bribed; he received the dead bodies into his boat, but never except by the express command of the judges. Even the Kings of Egypt were treated with this same severity.

Now we can judge the impressions that the symbolic figures <note>original: *Zinnebeeldige beeltenissen*; these are the hieroglyphic or emblematic representations used in ancient Egyptian religion.</note> must have made upon the understanding of our Egyptian worshippers. Those who are corrupted by their own desires abuse everything; and because that Script <note>original: *Schrift*; referring here to sacred hieroglyphic writing.</note> which was ordained for instruction brings them—through the effect of their indifference and as punishment for their godlessness—from error to error, it becomes for them an occasion for the most disastrous fall. Almost none of the common people who found themselves in the meeting place could read the common script; thus, one can be certain that none of them would have concerned themselves with understanding what the ancient script meant. They found themselves surrounded by symbols of great complexity. They were all images of men, women, and well-known animals. It is true that there are misshapen ones among them, and such that could evoke no properly distinct concept in them; yet the sight of the Sun, which often appeared at the top of their Tableaus <note>original: *Tafereelen*; large-scale painted or carved scenes, common in temple complexes.</note>, and upon the heads of the figures, evoked in them the idea of the Sun. A human or a bird placed within these images made them think of a human or a bird; and thus they remained very foolishly clinging to the image they saw before them, or to the name of "governor," or of "Sparrowhawk," <note>original: *Sperwer*; likely a reference to the hawk-headed god Horus, whose original symbolic meaning as a marker of time or seasonal cycles was being lost to literalism.</note>

They held the most notable representation—Osiris, the King or governor of the Seasons—to be the Leader and Father of all their Colonies; namely Cham <note>The biblical Ham, son of Noah, whom early modern historians often identified as the progenitor of the Egyptians and the origin of their "pagan" gods.</note>; whom they called Ham, Amoun, Hammon, and Thammus, according to the various pronunciations of the Provinces.

This Osiris, then, who was previously a <term>Symbolic Letter</term> <note>original: "Zinnebeeldige Letter"; an image used as a character or sign to represent a concept rather than a literal person.</note> or person, having become in the mind of the People an actual person—a Man who had formerly lived among them—his History was fashioned in relation to the attributes that were attached to his image. This was mingled with some traits of Cham's life; the rest was invented; and as many deeds were devised as there were objects found to be explained in the <term>Symbol</term> <note>original: "Zinnebeeldt"; a visual emblem or allegory.</note>, or ceremonies in the festivals, in which the sign of that glorious constellation <note>original: "gestermte"; here referring to the Sun as the primary heavenly body through which divine providence acts.</note>, by means of which God provides us with the necessities of life, was carried about. <margin>THE BIRTH OF THE GODS.</margin>

The Egyptians, who had now adopted the habit of worshipping the Sun as a God and as the cause of all good, and regarding Osiris as their founder, fell into a third error. They knew, through a confused memory and common usage, that this image of Osiris was related to the Sun; and indeed, according to the original Institution <note>original: "Instelling"; referring to the initial symbolic system established by the ancients before it was misinterpreted.</note>, this was the case. Moreover, they often saw the Circle—the sign of Divinity—placed upon the head of Osiris. For this reason, they constantly united the concept of Ammon with that of the Sun, and both of these with the concept of God: the Almighty and benevolent Being. 

They worshipped neither God nor the Sun without simultaneously singing the praises of the blessings of Osiris or Ammon. The one always corresponded inseparably with the other; this gave rise to the general rumor that Ammon or Osiris had moved into the Sun to take up his residence there, and that he did not cease from there to protect Egypt, taking pleasure in pouring out a much greater abundance upon that land, where...

## III.

### *Isis, the Queen of Heaven.*

After the symbolic King, or the mark of the Sun, the Egyptians had no sign that appeared so generally in their assemblies as *Isis*; the symbol of the Earth, or rather the announcement of the festivals marked by the products of the Earth in each particular season.

A waxing moon, or a full moon, placed on the head of Isis, or otherwise, could—as we have already seen—announce the festival of a New Moon; or the festival of the middle of the month, of the haymaking season, of the sowing season, of the harvest, or any other time of year; according to the accompanying <term>symbol; original: Zinnebeeldt</term> <note>In this context, a "symbol" or "emblem" served as a visual code to help a largely illiterate population track the liturgical and agricultural calendar.</note> that was specific to a particular season or product, and corresponded with a certain time of the year. But this writing was not uniform everywhere. The teachers of one province were inclined to write differently than those of other provinces; and instead of expressing the New Moon festivals, or the other parts of the month, by the figure of the Moon in such or such an appearance; they chose as the symbol of this heavenly body the animal that [can] see in the dark <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "kan" (can) indicates the sentence continues to describe an animal, likely a cat, which was associated with the moon and Isis/Bastet due to its nocturnal vision.</note>

Festivals of the Most High <note>The author likely refers to an original, singular concept of a supreme deity which he argues was later corrupted into the worship of celestial bodies.</note> were established for no other reason on the New or Full Moon, or on such a part of her course, than because those appearances are a natural summons, and an easy means, to gather the People on a fixed and announced day. But they lost sight of the adorable Being himself, the only object of the festivals; they believed that these festivals were dedicated to the Moon itself, and to that imaginary Woman, who they thought kept her residence there, and was very attentive to their needs. Everything, even the spots on the Moon, which through a false imagination show a Human face, served to strengthen them in their error. But is it indeed so easy to prove that the Phoenicians, the Syrians, the Greeks, and all the Western peoples were followers of the Egyptians? These latter traveled very seldom; content with the abundance they enjoyed at home, they could well do without foreign nations (a); and thus they did not go seeking elsewhere what they could gather without effort in their own land. For this reason, they seem little suited to serve as examples to other nations, or to share their ideas with them. Nevertheless, it is certain that Egypt has spread idolatry and superstitions everywhere. Let us begin by investigating what the means of that transmission was, so that we may subsequently discover the progression of that evil.

### VI.

#### *The Egyptian Gods, shared with Asia and Europe by the Phoenicians.*

<margin>
THE BIRTH OF THE GODS.
</margin>

Egypt was always, and still is, the most fertile land in the world. A sufficiently certain harvest—and one that was usually abundant far beyond the needs of the inhabitants—provided the opportunity for the establishment of vast granaries. These served as a refuge for the Arabs, the Canaanites, the Syrians, and the Greeks during years of famine. Travelers, driven there by necessity or curiosity, but especially the Phoenicians—who occupied only a small coastline near Lebanon and had no more reliable storehouse <note>The author uses "Magazyn," referring to a warehouse or supply center, highlighting Egypt’s role as the "breadbasket" of the ancient world.</note> than Egypt—were all equally impressed by the political order <note>original: "Staetkunde," referring to the sophisticated governance and civil administration of the Egyptian state.</note> that reigned in that excellent land. They were moved by the peaceful nature of the inhabitants; by the mysterious grandeur of the ceremonies and festivals celebrated there with great pomp; and finally, by the abundance they regarded as miraculous in a land where no rain falls. The idea they had of this river <note>Referring to the Nile.</note>, whose source remained unknown and whose flooding

After the Greeks had multiplied their Gods according to the number of symbols <note>original: *Zinnebeelden*, meaning emblems or allegorical representations</note> that they had allowed to be introduced into their land—without understanding the true meaning of them—they gave to each of these imaginary Gods nearly identical equipment to make their movement from one place to another easy, and to maintain their dignity. The pinnacle of all these follies—and it is a folly that had become universal—was not only intended to confuse God with that governor of the Stars and the Earth (that is to say, with the Sun), but even to seek that King, who had become the Leader of Nature, among their heroes or the founders of their state. ## XI.

### Deio, Dione, Diana, Hecate, Artemisia.

<margin>
BIRTH OF THE GODS.
</margin>

The common people have always loved ambiguities and wordplay; it has been so through all times and in all places. Just as a change in visual form has often caused several different gods to emerge from a single symbol <note>The author uses the term 'Zinnebeeldt' to refer to a symbolic image or emblem that carries a deeper religious or seasonal meaning.</note>, so too has a simple difference in name—or even just a different pronunciation of the same name—frequently produced a similar multiplication.

**Isis**, when taken as the Queen of Heaven or the Moon, was called **Echet**, **Hecate**, or **Achate**, meaning "the only one" or "the excellent" (a). Among some peoples of Syria, the same symbol was called, by a slight inflection of the name, **Achoth** (b), meaning "the Sister." This same figure, whom men had already made the consort of Jove <note>A name for Jupiter or the Sun in this context.</note>, or of the Sun, or of Jupiter (for up to this point, they are one and the same thing), likewise became his **Sister**.

But after Isis was deified, and she was seen as a woman or as a queen who resided in the moon and shared in the governance of heaven with Osiris or Adonis, the announcement of the return of the new moon—which was initially a very simple matter—took on a mysterious and weighty form and character: Hecate had become invisible for several days; her return was awaited with great solemnity. This goddess finally left the realm of the dead <note>original: *Ryk der dooden*</note> to return to heaven once more. Imagination found a vast field here to exercise itself; and since Hecate visited those two regions very regularly, journey after journey, one could not doubt that she ruled in heaven and in the invisible dwelling of the dead. On the other hand, the visible connection she had with the Earth and its produce—the various signs of which she always bore either on her head or in her hands—could not be unknown to them. And thus she became the threefold Diana, being at once: 1. the Earth; 2. the Moon, or the Mistress of Heaven; and 3. the Queen of the subterranean dwellings.

After so many different transformations of status <term>Staetsverwiffelingen</term> <note>Literally "state-revolutions," referring here to the various roles, titles, and identities a deity assumes over time.</note>, this Isis took on yet another new form; she became the famous Venus. This Venus presents in Antiquity, just as she still does today in the flattering language of our novels and theaters, two very different personas. At one moment she is the common Venus, the Goddess of the physical senses and the Mother of pleasure; then again she is the Heavenly Venus <term>Venus Urania</term> <note>From the Greek 'Ouranios' meaning 'Heavenly'; in classical thought, she represented spiritual or intellectual love as opposed to physical desire.</note>, who inspires wisdom and lifts the spirit to the most exalted contemplations, or to those beauties that concern the spiritual realm. They were also given, as we have seen in the History of Erichthonius <note>Erichthonius was a legendary early king of Athens, often cited in historical texts as a figure who established religious rites or festivals.</note>, **Symbolic Names** and duties.

From this it appears that everything was arranged for instruction; and that all the external aspects of Religion were like a substantial Preaching <note>The author suggests that ancient rituals were originally intended to be "sermons" that taught the people about nature and the seasons.</note>. That the Athenian Pallas and the goddess Pales, honored in the Palilia <note>A Roman pastoral festival held on April 21st, intended to purify both shepherds and their flocks.</note>, are the same can be judged from the similarity of their functions and names. Pales gave laws to the farmers of Italy; Pallas instructs in agriculture, as was appropriate for the Athenians. Both those names signify public order *(a)*. Now, the function of Isis was nothing other than *to manage public order* and to indicate the seasonal conditions of the year through a variety of displays or specific attributes that were unique to each particular season. Moreover, we also know historically, and according to the testimony of Diodorus Siculus <note>original: "Diodoor van Sicilien"; a Greek historian who wrote the *Bibliotheca historica* in the 1st century BCE.</note>, that the religion and the people of Athens originally descended from a colony that set out from Sais, a city in Lower Egypt; and that the Pallas of the Athenians was armed from head to toe because the Isis of Sais was also honored while being fully armed.

Scholars speak of Minos and of his Laws just as if the codex or body of them had been preserved in the public archives; and just as if they accurately knew the genealogy and the life of that Lawgiver. But how should one judge this in view of the circumstances that present themselves here? A King worshiped after his death; an empty tomb at which people gather to sing his praise; a Woman honored as the Mother of Fertility; a beloved Son who becomes a Lawgiver of the people: if we add to this the precise correspondence of the names Menes and Minos—such a similarity, corresponding in all respects between the Cretan festivals and those of the Egyptians, shows us abundantly that the former are a copy of the latter; and that all those personages, whose history has been so seriously recounted, never existed, and are nothing other than ancient symbols <term>Zinnebeelden: allegorical figures or emblems, often used in this period to explain how physical phenomena were personified as gods.</term> which have been mistaken for real persons.

### XVII.

---

(a) One may also note here that the Cretan Minos is not a man who actually existed; for his companions, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus, are nothing other than two words that signified something entirely different from a human being, but whose meaning was no longer understood. Since the name Menes or Minos was commonly used to signify the assembly over a deceased person—referring to the judgment held in both Crete and Egypt before the burial—it was called *the Court of Death*; *the judgment of sorrow*; or the *Sentence of those who sleep*; or the *judgment of the long Sleep*. All of this was expressed by the three words *Minos*, *Aeacus*, and *Rhadamanthus*. *Minos* and the *Manes* <note>The *Manes* were the chthonic deities or spirits of the deceased in Roman tradition.</note> were taken in the same sense to mean the funeral assembly, or death; <term>Aqa</term> <note>Hebrew: עקה; original Dutch: *Æaca* or *Gnaca*</note> signifies the most painful sorrow; <term>Redamim</term> <note>Hebrew: רדמים</note> signifies those who are in a deep sleep; and <term>Redameth</term> <note>Hebrew: רדמת</note> indicates a deep sleep.

People had retained from the ancient world the custom of lightly covering themselves with an animal skin, and of protecting themselves from the heat of the Sun under tents erected from stitched-together animal hides; an invention of one of the sons of Lamech*. 

<margin>* Jabal. Genesis 4:20.</margin>

After the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>, these remedies were found to be too weak against the piercing rains, the bitter cold, or violent winds. Men clothed themselves entirely in the skins of animals that they commonly used for food; primarily with the skins of bucks and goats, which are more pliable and softer than those of other beasts. Hunting sometimes provided more unusual, even elegant and venerable garments. He who appeared clothed in a lion or tiger skin drew the eyes of all toward himself and proclaimed a very useful victory. <note>In antiquity, wearing the pelt of a predator was a mark of a hero or protector who had cleared the land of dangerous animals.</note> Time and experience taught mankind to spin the wool of sheep and goats, and to prepare clothing from it that was softer and easier to wash.

## XXI.

### Vulcan, Hephaestus, Mulciber.

For what purpose shall we employ this strange figure that presents itself here? It is a comical posture, of which one leg, turned inward, is much shorter than the other. In his hand he holds a hammer, or pincers, or some other blacksmith's tool. He is identified as the husband of Venus; and he is given the names *Vulcan*, *Hephaestus*, or *Mulciber*. <note>original: "Vulcanus, Ephaištos, or Mulciber"</note> Those of Lemnos said that he was the son of Jupiter; and they recounted that his mother Juno, dissatisfied with his appearance, had kicked him out of Heaven with her foot; [that must have been a spiteful woman] <note>The author inserts this humorous remark on Juno’s famously vengeful character.</note> that he had been three days on his journey before he descended to the Earth; and that, falling upon their island, he had broken a leg from that violent fall. They added that a rare diligence compensated for his deformity; and that he consoled himself for his exile by devoting himself, in the caves of Mount Mosychlos, <note>original: "Berg Moſycles," a volcanic mountain on the island of Lemnos.</note> to the smelting of metals and the forging of all kinds of hand tools.

## XXII.

->*Atlas.*<-

Would there not also be a particular symbol <term>symbol; original Dutch: "Zinnebeeldt"</term> for the order of Priests, just as we have seen were established for the rural folk and the artisans or blacksmiths? The symbol intended for the governance of the Priests would probably not have been shown in public gatherings, but in the court or in the Labyrinth <note>The Egyptian Labyrinth was a massive complex of halls and courtyards described by ancient historians like Herodotus as surpassing even the Pyramids in wonder.</note>. And if another Horus <note>In this context, the author treats "Horus" not just as a single god, but as a title or a symbolic figure that changes attributes to represent different social functions or seasons.</note> were found who bore that mark, or who possessed visible characteristics suitable for the instruction of the Priestly order, all our previous reasonings would receive new strength due to the coherence and the connection in which everything would then be found.

It is known from the testimony of Herodotus; of Diodorus; of Plutarch; and of many other ancient writers, that study was the primary pursuit of the Egyptian Priests, who lived a very secluded life. They applied themselves to the knowledge of the order of the stars, the course of the planets, and of *Cuan* <note>original Hebrew: כון</note> or *Canan* <note>original Hebrew: כנן</note>, meaning *to prepare* or *to ripen* <note>original Latin: "expedire, maturare"</note>; from which comes *Wolcan* <note>original: עלכן "Wolcan"</note>, *the ripened work* <note>original Latin: "opus maturatum"</note>.

<summary>The author explores whether a specific symbolic figure, likely Atlas, served as the emblem for the Egyptian priestly class, mirroring the symbols used for farmers and smiths. It emphasizes the priests' scholarly dedication to astronomy and the linguistic roots of their sacred terminology.</summary>

Thus, for lack of Priests and formal instructions, Hercules stepped into the profession of Atlas and took that burden upon his own shoulders.

Horus thus received the name of *Eros*, or of *Hymeneus* <note>The Greek god of marriage ceremonies.</note>. In this way, Love appeared: now with the wings of the North-East wind; then with the club of Hercules; sometimes armed with the bow and arrow of Apollo, or of the Archer <note>The zodiac sign Sagittarius.</note>; also sitting on a Lion <note>The zodiac sign Leo.</note>; or leading a Bull <note>Taurus</note>, Ram <note>Aries</note>, Goat <note>Capricorn</note>, or two Fishes <note>Pisces</note>. These images gave rise to so many stories; the kingdom of Eros contained Heaven and Earth. Who could then still doubt that he ruled even to the bottom of the moist element? <note>A poetic reference to the sea or water.</note> The markers of the activities of each season, joined with the wedding torch, were held to be the monuments of his victories. He had disarmed all the gods; and their attributes in his hand became, first, the subject of the poets' play, and thereafter the profound speculations of the philosophers, who were a thousand times more ridiculous in that regard than the poets.

## XXIV.

->Proteus.<-

According to the fable, Proteus was the Guardian or shepherd of the <term>Sea-Calves</term> <note>These "sea-calves" are seals, which in classical mythology were said to be the flock of the sea god Neptune, tended by Proteus.</note>, who pull the Chariot of <term>Neptune</term> <note>The Roman god of the sea, equivalent to the Greek Poseidon.</note>: he took their count at the Island of Pharos, and gave them all equal refreshment; when one approached him, he changed himself into a Man or Woman, or Sheep, or Horse, into Liquid, or into such shapes as pleased him.

The truth of this matter is as follows: Proteus was the announcement of the time for the trading of the fruits of Egypt for Slaves, Cattle, Metals, Wine, and other Merchandise, which the <term>Phoenician</term> <note>An ancient seafaring civilization from the Levant, known as great traders across the Mediterranean.</note> Ships brought to the Island of Pharos, the only Egyptian Harbor that was safe at that time. These Ships took in their provisions of Grain, Flax, and all the products of Egypt in return. We have already seen before that the annual return of those ships to the outermost coasts of Egypt was announced by means of an <term>Osiris</term> <note>A major Egyptian deity; here, the author suggests a symbolic statue or marker of Osiris was used to signal the arrival of the fleet.</note>, whom they called Neptune. But since Idolatry or image-worship was introduced, Neptune—by the Egyptians, who held a hatred toward the Sea—was not

<margin>The Phoenix.</margin>
Since this, in their opinion, such a rare and significant event coincided with the rising of the desired annual North-Eastern Winds (*Etesian winds*); all of which they represented by a bird of singular beauty, which was wondrous among all others; and which arrived in Egypt after having spent 1461 years\* without appearing there.

## XXVI.

### Daedalus and Icarus.

After the Egyptians had changed the images, which they no longer understood, into so many objects of a detestable Religion, each region chose its own deity according to the inclination of the People toward this or that object. Such a Deity cured such a disease in such a place. Such a Goddess was, a little further on, the refuge in such another necessity: and so finally all of Egypt became full of Cereses, of Latonas, of Minervas, of Cybeles, and of Dianas; who, all taken together, were nothing other than Isis <note>In this context, the author refers to the Egyptian goddess Isis as the original "Key" or calendar sign that was later fractured into the many goddesses of Greek and Roman myth.</note>; the Key of the various festivals.

All of Egypt was filled with Advocates and Guardian Deities, who were very indulgent and well-disposed, and whose duties or occupations were regulated according to the needs of the Inhabitants. In Phoenicia <note>original: "Phenicien"</note>, and in Syria, the Emblems <note>original: "Zinnebeelden"; symbolic or allegorical images used to convey complex ideas.</note> had undergone the same Fate. The Manes <note>The author refers here to "Manes" not just as spirits of the dead, but as the sacred formulas and ancestral rites associated with them.</note>, or the festivals and institutions, were as well known in Sicily as in Crete; people spoke the same way at the festivals, without understanding the meaning. They were merely formulas of ceremony and custom. New cities were given names drawn from public worship, or from the ceremonies that were held in the highest regard; now, because these names were found to be exactly the same in very different places, the idea arose that people imagined the deeds and travels of figures from one coast to another. This was done to bring together and attach things that had no actual relation to one another, based solely on those coincidences.

In Attica and in the islands of the Archipelago, Icarus was known: yet under ideas that were very different from those of Crete. In those islands, it was understood that Icarus had been a husbandman <note>A husbandman is an archaic term for a farmer or cultivator of the land.</note>; they held a confused idea of the connection of *Mera* <note>original: "Mera"; refers to Maera, the dog of Icarius in Greek myth, often associated with the star Procyon.</note> with the *Dog Star* <note>The star Sirius.</note>, specifically when the North-East Winds (*Etesian winds*) did not accompany the appearance of that star; and of the sad condition into which the *Flight of Anubis* <note>In this context, the "flight" refers to the astronomical setting or disappearance of the symbol.</note> threw *Erigone*; that is, the loss of the harvest when the North-East winds did not cause the Nile to swell during the dog days. <margin>POETIC HEAVEN.</margin>From the History of Daedalus, and that of our two Icaruses <note>The author refers to two figures named Icarus: the son of Daedalus who flew too close to the sun, and Icarius, the father of Erigone mentioned in the previous section.</note>, one can easily judge how suspicious those fictions are at their core; and how greatly one can be mistaken if one wishes to find something historical in them; since the persons themselves had as little reality as their misfortunes.

In the time of Daedalus, according to the account of Diodorus of Sicily (a), statues had closed eyes and their hands fixed to their sides. However, Daedalus taught how one could make them with open eyes, with legs standing apart from each other, and with loose arms and hands, by which he became the wonder of everyone.

Many other writers testify to the old custom that the legs of images or statues were bound together, or even joined as if into one leg. These crude <term>ruwe: unrefined or primitive</term> beginnings, brought to perfection by Daedalus, are to some extent confirmed by various ancient statues. An Egyptian or Phoenician colony, which included all these depictions in the ceremonies of its religion, brought them along to Phocis <note>A region in central Greece</note>, specifically to the areas surrounding Parnassus and Delphi. It is true they had no meaning there; they bore no resemblance to anything that corresponded with that land. However, they had been honored for a long time alongside their leader as benevolent and favorable deities, and this was enough to establish the use of these images and the beautiful stories—

—an olive tree; and Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon, god of the sea</note> accompanied by a horse. Upon this they built the narrative of the struggle of the Athenian Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom</note> with Neptune, concerning which of the two would offer the most beautiful tribute to the New City, and thereby earn the privilege of giving it a name. It followed that the olive tree was judged to be of greater utility than the horse, and thus the Goddess achieved victory. Yet the meaning of this sculpture was very simple. It indicated either the two means of existence for the Athenians—namely, Agriculture and Navigation—or perhaps that they should value agriculture more highly than seafaring. Two or three examples of this kind are sufficient to clarify nearly all the ancient depictions that Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century CE</note> describes for us in his account of Greece, along with the fables that sprouted from them.

It is not unhelpful, as proof of what has been said, to note that one often finds the three Graces <note>The Charites: goddesses of charm, beauty, and nature</note> under the guidance of Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hermes; in this context, associated with the Egyptian Anubis or the star Sirius</note> in ancient depictions. This is because in Egypt, the three months of the flooding [of the Nile] follow the appearance of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, whose rising signaled the annual flooding of the Nile</note>. Similarly, the nine Muses <note>The goddesses of the arts and sciences</note> are found under the guidance of Horus-Apollo; this is because Horus, representing Labor, makes use of the nine following months of the year.

But what, then, was the reason that this Apollo gave oracles and predicted the future? This was precisely the primary purpose for which he was intended: Horus served no other purpose than to provide information—by means of his various attributes <note>original: "toevoegsels," referring to symbols or tools held by the figure</note>—regarding what work needed to be performed, and what one could expect according to the winds and the years. At that time, it was never forgotten that these depictions served as instructions for the Labor of the People. But after these symbols began to be viewed as Gods, people imagined that the depictions themselves knew the future and announced it to them. They stopped regarding them as convenient signs by which experienced men regulated the activities of the People and signaled in advance what had to be done from month to month. This matter of—

### XXIX.

### *The Furies, the Fates, and the Harpies.*

The division we have seen made of the twelve Isises <note>The author uses "Isises" to refer to the various symbolic female figures derived from the Egyptian goddess Isis</note> into three Charites <note>The Graces</note>, or three idle Nymphs under the guidance of Mercury; and into nine working ones under the guidance of Horus, we find confirmed by another division which, however different it may seem, nevertheless possesses a precise correspondence with the former. These are the three Graces, the three Furies; the three Fates <note>original: "Parken," referring to the Parcae or Moirae who spin the thread of life</note>, and the three Harpies <note>Monstrous winged creatures from mythology</note>. This second group of twelve strange figures is likewise nothing other than the succession of the months of Egypt, depicted according to the various seasons.

The Charites are, as we have seen, the "Isises"—or the markers—of the months of July, August, and September.

The three months of April, May, and June, and especially the latter two, being subject to storm winds—which sometimes overturned entire plains of olive trees and brought locusts and beetles from the heart of Africa that destroyed and spoiled everything—led the ancient Egyptians to give the three Isises <note>Plural of Isis, here referring to the seasonal markers or statues used to represent different months.</note> that announced these three months a female face, but with the body and claws of birds of prey. Birds were the common key to the meaning of the winds; and the name of Harpies, which they gave to these winds, was just like all the preceding ones, without any secret; meaning the locusts (a), or the plant-gnawing pests, which the aforementioned winds caused to emerge.

They called the heat *the Lion*, which is the zodiac sign that represents it; they called the winter the *Chimera*, or the Ibex, or wild goat, a sign still associated with this season <note>This refers to the constellation Capricorn, the "horned goat," which the sun enters during the winter solstice.</note>. Their third enemy, Trosibis, meaning *bad food* and likewise signifying the *tail of a serpent*, led them to form a monster out of all these parts, composed of the head of a lion, the body of a wild goat, and the tail of a serpent (a). But what are we to make of Bellerophon? Shall we seek his lineage in Corinth (b) and exhaust ourselves trying to fix the exact date of his exploits within the Julian period <note>A chronological system used by historians to reconcile different calendars by counting days from a fixed starting point in 4713 BCE.</note>? Bellerophon with his flying horse <note>Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology.</note> is nothing other than a ship, or the assistance of maritime trade, which brought to the colony of Lycia all sorts of refresh-

The fable of Perseus and Andromeda is likewise nothing more than a common figure of speech, from which a fable has been created. It was a common way of speaking among the Hebrews and Phoenicians to say that a city or a region was a "Daughter" of the rocks, the wildernesses, the rivers, or the mountains that surrounded it or that it contained. Thus Jerusalem is often called *the Daughter of Zion*; that is to say, *the Daughter of the dry place, or the Daughter of the barren hills, which she contained within her territory*. Palestine proper was, according to the account of Strabo *(b)*, a long coastline consisting of cliffs and a flat beach; it was bordered with rocks and sharp coastal reefs, from Joppa or Jaffa—which was essentially its only harbor—unto Gaza. The remainder, turning back toward stony Arabia, continues as far as Lake Sirbonides,

Since those of Colchis shared the same customs as the Egyptians, they undoubtedly used public signs to communicate their collective activities, in order to define the start and the duration of each task. Their river did not flood their farmlands as the Nile did in Egypt; however, at certain times of the year, it carried small gold flakes <note>original: *Lovertjes*, meaning small spangles or flakes of gold.</note> down to its banks, the collection of which enriched the inhabitants and contributed greatly to their livelihood. When the proper time for this collection arrived, it was of the utmost importance that this precious material was not allowed to drift away into the sea. To that end, people had to spread out along the banks of the Phasis <note>The Phasis, now the Rioni River in modern-day Georgia, was famous in antiquity for its gold-bearing sands.</note> at the right moment; they had to be ready to lay out sheepskins, still covered in wool, around the cliffs, under the roots of large trees, and in all the inlets of the river, so that the flakes would become entangled and remain there. The exact time for this work of such great consequence was announced by a public sign, consisting of a fleece accompanied by a snake or dragon. A fleece was displayed, and nothing was more natural in such a case than this sign. It was called the Golden Fleece; the

...for the continuation of the production of Yarn and Linen. For that reason it was necessary to *regulate sleep*, and to prescribe its measure. One was not permitted to sleep whenever one wished; everyone was subject to a certain *measure*, to a certain *hour*, and to a certain *regularity*.

This *measuring of Sleep* was then the primary concern of the People, and they spoke of nothing else. The Greeks, continually hearing the words *Jason (a)*—signifying *Sleep*—and *Mad* or *Mideh*, which signifies a *rule* or *regularity*; and furthermore hearing it said that *Jason*, guided by *Mideh*, had taken away the Golden Fleece; they embellished for themselves the Voyage with the Ship Argo, from the Greek coasts to the mouth of the Phasis <note>The Phasis is a river in Colchis, modern-day Georgia, where the Golden Fleece was said to be kept.</note>, and the conquest of the Golden Fleece, including the subduing of the terrible dragon that guarded it, by *Jason*, who had known how to please Princess Medea and had placed himself under her guidance in order to better achieve his aim <note>The author is arguing that "Medea" was not a historical princess, but a personification of the word "measure" (Mideh), referring to the disciplined schedule required for textile production.</note>. It is enough for us to have seen the first design of this fable. The ornaments added to it by the imagination of the Poets, or perhaps by idle travelers...

Circe is nothing other than the Egyptian Isis; who appeared in public announcements always in a distinct manner: now with a Nile-measure <note>a graduated rod used to track the rising of the river</note>; then with a distaff or weaver’s shuttle; then with a spear. She was always accompanied by the images of Horuses <note>the hawk-headed deity, often used here to represent various seasonal symbols</note>, and of other things that were changed from month to month, and sometimes even from day to day. She was the principal part of the Riddle <note>or symbolic puzzle</note>, to which the other mysterious parts were subordinate. She was always recognized; having with her, and as it were under her wand <note>meaning under her authority</note>, now a man with a dog's head <note>a reference to Anubis</note>; then a lion; then a snake or a tortoise; sometimes an entire child; at another time, the head of a child on the body of a snake; and furthermore the successive animals of the Zodiac; or others that announced the return of various agricultural tasks. In a word, she transformed everything that was near her into various animals. This Isis, and all that accompanied her, was thus a substantial Riddle to be explained; an emblem to be unfolded. But the word Circe, what does it mean? *The wrapping*, or *the Riddle* (a).

Let us go further. It is very probable that *Isis* received the name of *Circe* because of the *Circ*, or solar circle, which she commonly wore upon her head. That circle was the sign of the supreme being, whose various feasts *Isis* indicated. But why did they call this sun *Circ*, a riddle? Because one could not depict God; and the Solar Disk was the emblem of God. It was the emblem par excellence <note>original: "by uitneementheidt," meaning the preeminent or most excellent example</note>. The *Circ*. The place in Italy where this *Isis* with her circle on her head was brought and honored in ancient times, is still called *Monte Circello* <note>Mount Circeo, traditionally associated with the legend of Circe in the Odyssey</note> today. To announce certain feasts or offerings, which were perhaps celebrated in the evening at the appearance of the New Moon, or in the morning at the rising of a star, or of the *Planet Venus*—which displays a wondrous brilliance just before the arrival of the Dawn—they placed upon the head of *Isis*, instead of a solar ring, a star, or a known planet, or a waxing moon, or a full moon. These images, and the prayers sung in the Ancient Language at the return of each feast, gave rise to the thought that *Circe*, through her enchantments or mysterious words, had the power to make the stars and the moon descend to the earth. From time to time, people lost the meaning of these very simple symbols and of the names that were customary in the festivals, where everything had become an unchanging ceremony. Common script <note>The author likely refers to the transition from pictorial hieroglyphs to more abstract scripts like Demotic, where the visual connection to the original agricultural symbols was lost.</note> caused their meaning to be neglected; moreover, nothing contributed more to this forgetting than the habit of not calculating the sacred year accurately; instead, every four years, they allowed the start of the year to slip back by a whole day. <note>This refers to the Egyptian "Vague Year" of 365 days. Because it lacked a leap year, the calendar rotated through the seasons over a 1,460-year period (the Sothic cycle), meaning seasonal festivals eventually occurred at the "wrong" time of year.</note> Consequently, the festivals and symbols related to springtime labor eventually fell in the autumn or winter, and so on with the rest, until people no longer understood what all these things were actually intended to signify. All these images, being thus viewed as Men and Women whose deification festivals were being celebrated, were given a genealogy according to the order of their festivals. From whom, then, shall Osiris and Isis—that is to say, Jupiter and his wife <note>original: "Jupiter en zyne Vrouw". According to the order of the earliest times, a new Osiris and a new Isis—that is, the public notices of the New Year—appeared in the month of June or July. But according to the order of later times, these festivals did indeed follow one another in the same manner, yet in such a way that they fell in seasons and months with which they no longer had any proper connection <note>This refers back to the previous page's discussion of the Egyptian "Vague Year," where the lack of a leap year caused seasonal festivals to rotate through the calendar over centuries.</note>. Thus Sudek, or Cronus, or Saturn, became the father of Jupiter and Isis. Saturn, Rhea, Tethys, and Titan were their ancestors: the Titans were regarded as the sons of Ur, or Urania, and Ops. Most genealogists lean in that direction. Others, like Diodorus <note>original: "Diodoor", referring to Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote extensively on Egyptian mythology.</note>, make Urania and Ops the children of Acmon; the Egyptians, in their genealogy, climb up to Vulcan. Acmon the Coppersmith, therefore, and Vulcan are one and the same.

<margin>The origin of the historical elements discovered within fables.</margin>
From these things, it is clear that neither Holy Scripture nor History provided the material or the occasion for these inventions. Rather, once idolatry and myths were already born, the peoples—who still retained confused ideas of some ancient truths—applied them to such fables as seemed to have some correspondence with them. In this manner, the true and the false were mixed together; and thus one can still recognize the footsteps of history within the body of fables; indeed, even such testimonies that agree in all respects with the Origin of the World and of Nations, in the manner that Moses relates them to us.

This absurd opinion <note>The author reflects an Enlightenment-era view, treating ancient mythology as a series of logical errors or "absurdities" resulting from the loss of the original meaning of symbolic language.</note> became as common as the language and the images that had given rise to it. The transmigration <term>Zielsverhuizing: also known as metempsychosis, the belief that the soul moves into a new body after death</term> of the souls of Osiris and Isis into various animals before their arrival in the stars found favor among the people and was regarded as an indubitable history; indeed, it was seen as the precept, or model, of the general opinion regarding the state of souls after death. No one in Egypt doubted any longer whether the soul of man, when it separated from the body, passed into that of another human or animal; from this again into another; then again into a third, and so on through a long series of penance to atone for the evil it had committed: after which it finally, purified of its faults and released from its desires, passed into such a star or planet as was assigned to it for its residence.

### XL.

<margin>POETIC HEAVEN.

*The Sun.</margin>
Nothing was simpler, nor more ingenious, than the astronomical language; which at a glance sketched out the seasons and the tasks specific to each of them, by making the ruler of the Earth <note>The Sun; the original margin note identifies "De Zon" (The Sun) as the ruler mentioned here.</note> pass through twelve houses; named the Ram, the Bull, the Lion, the Balance, etc.: all of which are names that have a precise relation to what occurred successively upon the Earth during the course of the whole year.

<margin>a. Orbit, revolution.

b. Renewal.

c. Passage of the Soul from one body into another.</margin>
But nothing was also more clumsy and wretched than the historical sense <note>In this context, "historical sense" refers to the mistake of interpreting symbolic or metaphorical stories as literal, factual history.</note> that the common people, in subsequent times, attributed to this language; and such was evidently the origin of the ridiculous doctrine of the Transmigration of Souls <term>Zielsverhuizing: metempsychosis, or the belief that the soul moves into a new body (human or animal) after death</term>, which Pythagoras brought from Egypt into Italy as a rare discovery. These trifles, dressed up with the high-flown words of *Periclosis* <note>original: *Periclosis*; a Greek-derived term referring to a cyclical circuit or revolution</note>; a, *Palingenesis* <note>original: *Palingenesis*; Greek for "rebirth" or "regeneration"</note> b; and *Metempsychosis* <note>original: *Metempsychosis*; Greek for the movement of a soul into a new body</note> c; met with great success among the philosophers; and this is still the teaching of the Indian masters; we also know more than one scholar who speaks of this transmigration of souls with nothing but respect.

## Religious Honor Paid to the Animals.

The natural consequence of this sentiment <note>The author refers to the doctrine of the transmigration of souls mentioned on the previous page.</note> was the sparing of the blood of animals, despite the fact that God placed them among us to serve us and to provide our nourishment. It is true that weighty reasons were devised to ensure the people were not deprived of the meat of oxen, which provides an abundant and perfect food. It is also true that there was a kind of tacit agreement between the provinces of Egypt, where one province would use the meat of sheep and another the meat of goats, so as not to be deprived of a profitable trade <term>Koophandel: commerce or mercantile exchange</term>, or to avoid having too much supply at once. However, the Egyptian priests generally abstained from eating any meat, regardless of the animal; and in general, all those animals after which the constellations <term>Gesterntens: the stars or zodiac signs</term> were named were regarded with reverence by the Egyptians, as having been the first refuge of their gods, and as potentially still being the dwelling place of the souls of their deceased parents.

Now one regarded with nothing but a religious awe those animals in which it was known—without any possibility of doubting it—that Osiris and Isis <note>The primary god and goddess of the Egyptian pantheon, often associated with the sun and moon respectively.</note> had made their dwelling place; such as the Ram, the Bull, the Heifer, the Goat, and the Lion. The ancient custom of parading in ceremony, during the festivals of certain seasons, that animal which gave its name to the heavenly house <term>Heemel-huis: a zodiac sign or astrological house</term> into which the sun then entered, persuaded the people of certain regions to honor especially that creature which was carried about at the festival falling at the end of their harvest. Thus the Ram became the beloved animal of the inhabitants of Thebes, whose harvest ended around the entry of the Sun into the Ram <note>The constellation Aries</note>. The Ox and the Calf became the most favored animals of the inhabitants of Memphis, whose harvest ended when the Sun entered the Bull <note>The constellation Taurus</note>. Those of Mendes, living close to the sea and whose harvest occurred later—namely, around the entry of the Sun into the Goats or Twins—had, according to the account of Herodotus*, a special reverence for goats.

The image of the Ox and the Calf was, among all the symbols <term>Zinnebeelden: symbolic images or emblems used to represent abstract ideas or natural forces</term>, the one most suited to the taste of the people. The reason for this is that it was the animal that appeared during the Harvest festival in the most prominent region of Egypt, namely at Memphis. The concept of fertility became inseparable from the sight of the Ox. People gave the Nile a Bull’s head to signify that the river was the Father of the Egyptian harvests. From this practice arose the custom of depicting other rivers—which do not flood the lands as the Nile does, but nonetheless do not fail to fertilize the fields and estates they flow through—in the same bull-like manner <note>original: "Sic tauriformis volvitur Aufidus." — A reference to Horace's Odes, describing the river Aufidus (now the Ofanto in Italy) as "bull-formed," a poetic convention borrowed from the Egyptian association between rivers and bulls.</note>.
