The inhabitants of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in Ancient Egypt.</note>, who formed a distinct Dynasty or Kingdom separate from that of Memphis, believed they stood in high enough favor with the Sun—after whom their capital was named—to receive a share of his visit, or that of his Son. Thus, they soon possessed, just like those of Memphis, their own sacred Ox. They gave him the name of *Menavis*, or *Menevis*, which is the same as *Menes* the Strong, or the same as *Menophis* <margin>* See above, page 167.</margin>; and by selecting a distinct name for him in this way, they also attributed to him other qualities and other specific duties,

<meta>catchword: who/which</meta>

Mr. de Maillet <note>Benoît de Maillet (1656–1738), a French diplomat and author known for his descriptions of Egypt.</note>, in his *Description of Egypt*, 7th Letter, believes that Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> intended to say that after the death of the reigning King, the Priests received knowledge from the mixture of colors on the skin of Apis as to who the deceased King's successor should be; and that they had thereby found a means to make themselves masters of the Throne’s succession. However, it appears clearly enough that Strabo in that passage is not speaking of the successor to the King, but rather of the successor who had to be placed in the stead of Apis, who had been drowned in the water during the ceremony, or had died a natural death. The selection of this Calf occurred according to the evidence of its spots.

<margin><note>original: "λυκός, Lycos, Lupus"</note> Wolf</margin>
There was also, in a region of Lower Egypt, a symbolic figure used to represent the Year, or the succession of the twelve signs of the heavens. When this image was no longer understood, it gave rise to the specific honoring of the Wolf and the sharing of its name with the city of Lycopolis <note>A city in Upper Egypt, known today as Asyut, where the wolf-headed god Wepwawet was worshipped.</note>, and subsequently with Lycia, the Lyceum, and various places in Greece, primarily in Arcadia. It is well known that wolves have the habit of walking in a file, one after another. A proverb has even been made of it; and among naturalists <note>Historical observers of nature and wildlife.</note>, it is a common observation that wolves, when crossing a river, follow one another in a line, with the second holding the tail of the first, the third holding that of the second, and so on. This figure was chosen to signify the Year, because the year is composed of twelve months that immediately follow one another. The truth of this is so clear that the Greeks gave the Year the name *Lycabas* <note>A poetic Greek word for "year," which some ancient authors incorrectly linked to the word for wolf (*lykos*).</note>, meaning the *Wolf-walk* <note>original: "Wolvengang"</note>.

Another circumstance that is peculiar to the institution of the Jewish Passover is the prohibition against boiling the meat of the Passover Lamb, and against eating any part of it raw. What interest could the religion of the Hebrews have in the offering being roasted and not boiled; and what was the necessity for the prohibition against eating raw meat, for which one naturally has an aversion? We can judge the customs of the Egyptians from those of the Athenians, who were one of their colonies. When these [Athenians] offered sacrifices to Horus or to Hores—that is, to the Seasons <note>The author links the Egyptian deity Horus with the Greek *Horae* (the Seasons), suggesting a shared mythological origin in solar and agricultural cycles.</note>; gods who undoubtedly originated from Egypt—the custom of that idolatrous act was *to boil the meat* (a) *and not to roast it.* In Athens, they maintained the Egyptian custom in the service of those gods who clearly had come from Egypt; and the Hebrews were commanded to do the opposite, so that they should not appear to have any part in the idolatrous practices and customs. The prohibition against eating any part of the Lamb that was raw—for example, the entrails—referred to the excessive custom...

Origin of Amulets, or protective charms worn around the neck.

<margin>
* A fending off of evils <note>original: "Amolimentum malorum"</note>
</margin>

This custom of curbing the powers of the Enemy <note>The "Enemy" refers to Typhon, the deity of drought and chaos</note>, and hanging a bound Typhon around the necks of Children, the Sick, and the Dead, seemed so salutary and so important that it was also adopted by other Nations. Children and the sick commonly wore a small plate upon which the T. was placed, which was regarded as a powerful preservative. In time, instead of the Letter T.—which was first engraved on that plate, but whose sense and meaning were not understood by other peoples—other characters were used. Sometimes a Snake, a Harpocrates <note>Harpocrates was the Greek adaptation of the Egyptian child-god Horus; he was often depicted with a finger to his lips, which the Greeks misinterpreted as a symbol of silence</note>, or an object of common devotion was placed upon it; sometimes even ridiculous, indeed most indecent figures. But the name of *Amulets*, given to that plate, which carries the meaning of the fending off of evil, very naturally reveals the intention of the Egyptians, from whom this custom originates.

From this we see the improper use they made of these images, which in their original institution <term>institution: The primary establishment or original intended purpose of a symbol</term> related to the Nile, to agriculture <note>original: "Akkerbouw"</note>, and to matters entirely foreign to the interpretations of later times. Behold there, most likely, a first Key with which one might undertake to explain some parts of the meaning that the Egyptians of later times assigned to their sacred script <note>Hieroglyphics</note>, or figurative language. But it is plain enough that everything therein related to the false ideas they had derived from the ancient images; and furthermore, there is far too little to be gained from such investigations to spend even the slightest labor upon them.

In this way, education assumed a hidden and solemn character, without destroying anything that the People believed. It only proclaimed a more perfect state and such knowledge as one could not attain except through trials and exertions of strength that were incompatible with the condition of the common man. By this means, they prevented the people from erupting into fury. Yet this was already a great injustice on the part of the Priests—that they held the truth captive and claimed it for themselves alone, to the exclusion of all others.

Origin

The Ceres of Sicily and of Eleusis is nothing other than the Egyptian Isis; brought to those places by Phoenician merchants, who enriched themselves by transporting grain from Lower Egypt to those places where the demand for provisions drew them; and in general to the various coasts of the Mediterranean Sea, where they had warehouses and settlements. Under the hands of these merchants, the ceremonial of the agricultural festivals <note>Dutch: *Landfeesten*</note> had acquired a different form, whether differing by much or by little. The Mother of the Harvest <note>Ceres</note> mourned her daughter <note>Proserpina</note> among them, instead of, according to the Egyptian ceremonial, mourning her husband <note>Isis mourning Osiris</note>. Except for this, the basis and meaning were exactly the same; the one allusion as well as the other had a visible relation to the sad change that the Earth had undergone through the Deluge, and to the difficult progress of agriculture <note>Dutch: *Akkerbouw*</note>, the regularity and rules of which had cost much time.

That was the name of *Ceres*, meaning *destruction, breach, or overturning* (a). This solitary Mother bewails the loss of her dear Daughter; that is, she laments the lost Abundance—the ancient fertility which the waters rising from the depths of the Earth had taken from her. She mourns the grain that is covered and mixed with a multitude of noxious plants that choke it, or that is uselessly scattered in barren fields.

Another depiction was called Celeus: this was a Horus who represented the collection of agricultural tools, brought to perfection through continued use. Instead of adhering to this original simplicity, the Greeks devised a thousand trifling stories about each of these names; they transformed them into various historical persons who were said to have lived and ruled in *Eleusis* <note>An ancient city near Athens, famous for the initiation ceremonies known as the Mysteries</note> or in the surrounding neighborhood.

<margin>Preparations for the Mysteries.</margin>
The festival, in which the memorials of the ancient state of the human race were preserved, was renowned in Egypt, in Phoenicia, and in Sicily. From those places, it passed with all its various rituals into Greece; but just as the features of the symbolic painting gave the Greeks an opportunity to imagine as many persons and distinct events as there were elements in that painting, so too did the virtuous customs inherent to those festivals give rise to a thousand bustling ceremonies. These lessons and preparations have been preserved in the great festivals and have come down to us. 

But the religious spirit that had once animated them became lost among most nations. They degenerated into mere customs without spirit; and subsequently, those practices were regarded as the most important part of the divine service. In their origin, they were—just as they still are among us—either the outward expressions of <term>piety<note>original: *Godvrucht*; a sincere, internal devotion to the divine</note></term> or the means to encourage it. Now, however, they were held as sources of merit in themselves; people placed their trust in them; they sought new inventions and added something to them from year to year and from country to country. 

People believed themselves to be devout in proportion to how much they multiplied these practices: to be certain of the success of one's performances, one only needed to be able to count so many days, so many hours, so many formulas, such a number of prayers. These things being performed, the gods had to be satisfied; and by this means, people assured themselves of an eter—

<margin>**POETIC HEAVEN.** The Altar-servant.</margin>
The Torch-bearer (a); he is the same as the Egyptian Osiris; that is, the Sun. 
The third persona, whom one called the *Altar-servant*, the *Worshipper* (b); was held by the Greeks to represent the Moon, because he wore a crescent moon upon his head; but right here, one sees that this persona was Isis. Now we know that Isis with her crescent moon does not signify the Moon itself, but rather the New Moon festival, or the establishment of the various festivals to praise God for all the products of the Earth. And that is the reason why this third persona kept himself close to an Altar and was called the *Worshipper*.

<margin>The sacred Interpreter, or Messenger.</margin>
The fourth was called the *Messenger of the Gods* (c), or Hermes; which corresponds with the Egyptian Anubis. Now this Anubis with his dog's head, and his Nile-measure, accompanied by two Snakes, is nothing other than the beneficial report that the dog-star <note>The star Sirius, whose rising heralded the annual flooding of the Nile, crucial for Egyptian agriculture</note> gives in due time, in order to secure oneself and provide for one's livelihood through the observation of the rising of the Waters. After the most carefully selected sacrificial animals <term>Offerdieren; animals chosen specifically for ritual slaughter</term> had been killed, it was still not felt that enough had been done. They examined the entrails <note>original: "Ingewanden"; the internal organs, particularly the liver, heart, and lungs, used for divination</note>, which were removed in order to cook the meat; and if any defect, injury, or unhealthiness was found therein, they believed that nothing had been accomplished. But when everything was healthy, and the internal parts as well as the external were found to be without flaw, they believed that the gods were satisfied <margin>* *Litazisse*, meaning the gods were appeased: having performed acceptable sacrifices.</margin> <note>original: "Litazisse," a Dutch rendering of the Latin "litasse," meaning to have sacrificed with favorable omens.</note>, and that all duties had been perfectly fulfilled, because nothing had been lacking in the outward ceremony. <margin>DIVINATION.</margin>

These foolish rubricators <term>rubricariften; those who obsessively follow formal rules or "rubrics" of ritual</term> placed the entirety of perfection in a precise knowledge of the rules that governed the selection and general examination of the sacrificial animals <term>Offerdieren; animals specifically chosen for ritual slaughter</term>. Their primary principle consisted in this: that the perfect or defective state of the exterior and the entrails <note>original: "Ingewanden"; the internal organs, such as the liver or heart, used for fortune-telling</note> was the sign of either complete agreement or complete opposition on the part of the Gods. 

Consequently, everything became a subject of observation. Everything in the sacrificial animals, which now stood ready to be slaughtered, seemed significant and weighty to them, as well as in the birds that wander through the air. All the movements of an ox being led to the altar <note>original: "Autaer"</note> became so many prophecies <note>original: "Voorzeggingen"</note>: did it go there peacefully, straight ahead, and without any resistance? That was the omen that one would succeed in one's affairs easily and without opposition. Its wildness, its deviations, its manner of falling, or its attempts to defend itself gave rise to so many favorable or unfavorable interpretations. In short, they made everything count, whether good or bad, through vain and trifling similarities and mere hair-splitting <term>Muggezifteryen; literally "straining at gnats," meaning excessive attention to trivial details</term>.

### Sorceries.

</margin>

The arrangement of leaves, neatly joined together to distinguish the meaning of the specific items to which they were attached, gave rise to the belief that such combinations of plants possessed great power over health, even when they were not applied as a literal medicine. Furthermore, because observers could see no logical connection between certain branches of plants—placed this way or that—and the healing or the successful harvest that was believed to be the result, they could find no other explanation than to attribute the primary power to the combination of very ancient and unintelligible words. These words were pronounced or chanted by the priests as they carried those <term>emblems <note>The Dutch *Zinnebeelden* refers to symbolic representations or allegories used by the priesthood to communicate with the public.</note></term> before the people with great solemnity. 

The matter was simple in itself: that foliage and the formula of proclamation served only to inform the bystanders of a Truth, a festival, or a collective task that was to be performed uniformly by all. Later, however, when neither the emblem nor the proclamation—which people always observed as a religious duty— <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "un-" suggests the next page continues with "unintelligible" or "understood."</note>

From this, our philosopher—through a manner of reasoning that, however perverse it might be, found much acceptance—formed a conclusion: that the child who came into the world at the same moment when the first star of Aries appeared above the horizon would undoubtedly be rich in livestock; and in the same manner, they proceeded with the others.

Since this entire distribution was still new—consisting only of those five deities who were of much later times than the birth of the Egyptian gods—one should not be surprised that people moved entirely away from the ancient use of symbols (<term>Zinnebeelden</term> <note>The author uses this term to describe allegorical or symbolic images that represent abstract ideas</note>). In the very first use of these depictions, the circle did not mean the Sun itself, but God. It was merely a symbol for Him, and the form of the circle, in its origin, signified nothing other than the symbol *par excellence*. The depiction of a waxing Moon did not signify the Moon itself either, but rather the time of the New Moon and the assembly [of the people] on the first day of the month. Similarly, the T-shape <note>Likely referring to the 'cross' at the bottom of the Venus symbol ♀, which the author interprets as an ancient Nilometer or measuring tool</note> that is placed under the sign of the planet Venus, and the serpent-staff (<term>Caduceus</term> <note>The staff carried by the god Mercury, traditionally entwined with two snakes</note>) given to Mercury, were originally just measures of the swelling of the Nile and the notice to pay attention to it. Yet here, these two additions are interpreted differently: one as the mark of a heavenly messenger, the other as a signifier of evil—meanings devised in later times, which are far removed from the clear and original purpose of these Celestial Symbols.

The conclusion one can draw from the testimony of Herodotus and several others is this: because the Egyptian nation remained steadfast in its customs—despite the whimsical interpretations they later applied to them—one may believe that the Egyptians from the most ancient times counted their days in cycles of seven. But where does this custom come from? Do they owe it to the Hebrews? Or did the Hebrews receive it from them? Both claims are equally false.

The Egyptians, having preserved the primary customs of the most ancient times better than other pagan nations, arrived at this practice—and indeed without any deliberate intent on their part—because they regulated their astronomy and the order of their days according to the number seven, just as was done in the time of Noah, and even in the time of Adam. ### *The Fatal \* Influences.*

The human intellect; always readier to draw correct conclusions from a false premise than to ensure the truth of the premise itself; had no sooner invented this trifling correspondence between the metals and the planets, based solely on the character of the Gods whom one had made to dwell within them; but, seeing one metal abundant in one land and another metal in a different climate, it immediately drew the conclusion that the Planet which undoubtedly favored the production of that metal there held dominion over that entire region. Every country thus had its ruling Planet; whose power one extended over the animals, and even over the inclinations of the Mind. In one land, everything was Lead. In another land, everything was Quicksilver. Gradually, the system of the Planets was used to account for everything. But the recurrence of the seven-times-seventh <note>The number 49 (7x7) was historically considered a "Grand Climacteric," a year of great physical or spiritual danger.</note>, which one called the fatal recurrence (*Climacteric*) (a), was, and is still in many minds, a dangerous year, a decisive day (*critical*), or an hour for which one congratulates oneself if one has escaped it.

The Climacterics, or fatal recurrences, seemed to be momentous events and circumstances that exerted a powerful influence on the sick, on the state of private individuals, on the fortune of Princes, the fate of wars, and on the stability of States. ## XII.

### *Origin of Alchemy.*

Each festival gradually acquired a specific <term>ceremonial</term> <note>The formal sequence of rites and actions performed during a religious service.</note>, its own displays, and an altar of a particular nature. That altar was surrounded by foliage, and that foliage or those leaves soon changed, just as the appearance of the altars did. At such a festival, a wreath of oak leaves was appropriate; at another, a myrtle wreath. In one place, the altar had to be made of stone; elsewhere of wood; sometimes it was formed from a single sod of earth or a clump of clay, encircled by a garland of common herbs.

What had once been adopted during a significant circumstance became thereafter a custom, and eventually even a law. The number, the symbols, and the histories of the objects regarded as gods subsequently gave rise to a hundred variations, which appeared to be very important regulations and necessary precautions. Anyone who failed in even a single point of the prescribed ceremony could expect nothing less than a plague or famine; indeed, if the offended gods sent such a person only a passing storm or some rampaging beast, he got off lightly for his mistake. It is certain that these words did not have the slightest relevance or connection to the undertaking about which consultation was being sought. Yet they were twisted into so many turns, and dragged in so much by the hair <note>A translation of the Dutch idiom "er bij het haar bijslepen," meaning to force a connection or include something irrelevant to support an argument.</note>, that they necessarily had to yield somewhat to the subject; and in this manner, it happened not infrequently that some appearance of relevance or correspondence was found in them. 

In place of the aforementioned methods, people also frequently resorted to <term>the Lot: a form of sortition or divination by chance, similar to drawing straws, where the outcome is believed to be determined by a higher power.</term>; consisting of a certain number of slips of paper, laden with random words, or perhaps verses, which were either well-known or newly composed. These slips being thrown into a box and well shaken, the first one drawn out was solemnly delivered to the distressed family as a means of their reassurance.

But one might say: it is clear enough that the practices of which we have spoken were quite capable of spreading everywhere those foolish ideas—which are still cherished among the common people today—namely, that one can maintain communication with the dead, and that they frequently come to bring us reports. If I could yet provide my readers with the evidence of this custom, or rather of that perverted misuse of funeral ceremonies <note>original: *Lykceremonieel*</note>; I would, in my judgment, have shown more than enough that the sentiments of men concerning the gods, the dead, and the answers received from both, are nothing other than a literal and clumsy interpretation of very simple signs, and even simpler ceremonies, which served to make known certain truths or to fulfill certain duties.

->א (Aleph)<-

**אבאישתא** *Ebbaiftho*, or *ephaisto*, the Father of Fire. Page 277 <note>original: "de Vader des Vuurs". The author is likely drawing a connection to the Greek god Hephaestus.</note>
**אב גרות** *Ab Gerooth*; *ab Garüs*, Father Gradivus. 269 <note>Latin original: "Gradivus pater." Gradivus is an epithet of the Roman god Mars, meaning "the Marcher."</note>
**אב יד** *Abiir*, *abirecha*, your strong one; Apis. 399 <note>original: "uwe sterke". Apis refers to the sacred bull of Egyptian mythology, here being etymologically linked to the Hebrew word for "mighty" or "bull."</note>
**אבש** *Abash*, to rot, to become moldy. 373 <note>Latin original: "putrescere, Mucidum fieri."</note>
**אובש** *Obs*, Moldiness, *Obshu pherudooth*. Joel 1:17. ibid. <note>Latin original: "Mucor". The Hebrew phrase from Joel 1:17 is typically translated as "the seeds shrivel" or "rot under their clods."</note>
**אוב** *Obb*, Leviticus 20:27. Swelling, puffing up. 62 <note>original: "Opswelling, opblasing." In biblical Hebrew, "Ob" refers to a medium or a spirit of the dead, but the author here provides an etymological sense of inflation or expansion.</note>
**אגמ** *Agam*, Pond, *Agmoon* and *Acmon*, Job 41:11. a spacious Kettle, the Brazen Sea. 372 <note>The "Brazen Sea" refers to the great bronze basin in Solomon's Temple. Job 41:11 (or 41:20 in some versions) describes a boiling pot or cauldron.</note>
**אדר** *Adar*, or *eder*, excellence, *Adrefta*, excellence of the Fire. 91. <note>original: "uitnementheidt".</note>
*Adar*, great, and *Mad*, Measure, Hem. From this comes *Adromad*, that is, Andromeda, a long Coast. 347 <note>original: "Adromad, dat is, Andromeda, een lange Kust." The author suggests a Phoenician origin for the Greek mythological name Andromeda, interpreting it as a geographical description.</note>

**Corban** <note>original Hebrew: קרבן</note>, **Offering**, **Gift**, **Sacrifice** <note>original Latin: *Oblatio*, *Donum*, *Sacrificium*</note>. Leviticus 6:20. Mark 7:12. The **Corybantes**, offerers from the island of Crete. 232 <note>The author suggests the Corybantes, the armed and dancing attendants of the goddess Cybele, take their name from the Hebrew word for sacrifice.</note>

**Keri** <note>original Hebrew: קרי; meaning "opposition" or "contrary"</note>, and **Ber**, **Kerber**, or **Cerberus**. 140 <note>A linguistic link is proposed between a Hebrew root and the three-headed hound of Hades.</note>

**Keren** <note>original Hebrew: קרן</note>. **Splendor** <note>original Latin: *Splendor*; the Hebrew word *Keren* can mean "horn" or "ray of light," hence the traditional depiction of Moses with horns.</note> 376

**Kerets** <note>original Hebrew: קרץ</note> or **Ceres**, **Breaking**, **Destruction** <note>original Latin: *Confractio*, *Excidium*</note>. Jeremiah 46:20. 444 <note>The author links the goddess of agriculture, Ceres, to a Hebrew root meaning to nip or destroy, citing a passage in Jeremiah regarding a "destruction" or "stinging fly" from the north.</note>

**Kereth** <note>original Hebrew: קרת</note>, or **Kartha**, a **City**, **Harpocrates**. 108

**Kereth** <note>original Hebrew: קרת</note>, **City** <note>original Latin: *Civitas*</note>, the **Curetes**. 231 <note>The Curetes were mythological mountain-dwelling guards of the infant Zeus; here they are linked to the Hebrew word for a city or settlement.</note>

-> R <note>The Hebrew letter Resh (ר)</note> <-

**Ruach** <note>original Hebrew: רוח</note>, the **Wind**, the giant **Roechus**. 253 <note>Likely referring to the giant Rhoecus from Greek myth, here derived from the Hebrew word for wind or spirit.</note>

**Rasah** <note>original Hebrew: רזה</note>, **To make thin** <note>original Latin: *Emaciare*</note>, **Atrophy** <note>original Greek: *atrophia*</note>, **leanness** <note>original Latin: *macies*</note>. 343

**Rachal** <note>original Hebrew: רכל</note>, **marcol**, **marcolet**. Ezekiel 27:24. Leviticus 10:16. **Mercurius** <note>The god Mercury</note>. 302 <note>The Hebrew root *Rachal* refers to trade or peddling; the author links this to Mercury, the Roman god of commerce and merchants.</note>

**Raha** <note>original Hebrew: רעה</note>, or **Ragna**, **Rhea**. 195 377 <note>The author connects a Hebrew root—possibly meaning to feed/pasture or perhaps a variant of "evil"—to the Titaness Rhea.</note>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index of the work, moving from the Hebrew letter Resh (ר) mentioned in the previous page's summary—though that section is skipped in the current transcription—to the final letters of the Hebrew alphabet: Shin (ש) and Tav (ת). The author continues his project of "sacred philology," attempting to find the Hebrew origins of Greek mythology, celestial names, and various classical concepts.</meta>

# I N D E X .

->ש<- <note>The Hebrew letter Shin</note>

**Shibbul** <note>original Hebrew: שבל</note>, **Shibboleth**, **Ear of Grain** <note>original Latin: *Spica*; original Dutch: *Koorn-air*</note>. 519

**Shoter** <note>original Hebrew: שטר</note>, **Judge** <note>original Latin: *Judex*</note>. Joshua 1:10. 377

**Shichor** <note>original Hebrew: שיחור</note>. **Sirius**, the **Dog Star**, the **Nile**. Jeremiah 2:18. 43 <note>The name Shichor, meaning "black" or "turbid," was a Hebrew name for the Nile; the author links it here to the star Sirius, which heralded the river's flooding.</note>

**Shir** <note>original Hebrew: שיר</note>, **Hymn** <note>original Latin: *Hymnus*</note>, and **Ranan** <note>original Hebrew: רנן</note>, to **sing**, to **rejoice**, the **Sirens**. 367 <note>The author suggests the mythological Sirens derive their name from Hebrew roots for singing and joyful shouting.</note>

**Shelav** <note>original Hebrew: שלו</note>, **Salvation** <note>original Dutch: *Heil*; original Latin: *Salus*</note>, **Quail** <note>original Latin: *Coturnix*</note>. 260 <note>In the Exodus narrative, quails were provided to the Israelites; the author appears to link the bird's name to a root for well-being or safety.</note>

**Shelang** <note>original Hebrew: שלג; likely referring to *Sheleg*, snow</note>, or **Shelaw**, **Flint** <note>original Latin: *Silex*</note>. 351

**Sphang** <note>original Hebrew: שפע; *Shefa*</note>, to **overflow**. From this comes the Egyptian **Sphinx**. 58 <note>Early modern scholars often linked the Sphinx to the abundance (*Shefa*) brought by the overflowing of the Nile.</note>

<column-break/>

->ת<- <note>The Hebrew letter Tav</note>

**Tophet** <note>original Hebrew: תופת</note>. 180 <note>A location in Jerusalem associated with child sacrifice and later used as a metaphor for Hell.</note>

**Thelah** <note>original Hebrew: תלה; *Talah*</note>, to **Suspend** <note>original Latin: *Suspendere*</note>. Job 26:7. To **extend** or **spread out**. 281

**Tham** <note>original Hebrew: תם</note>. **Perfection**, combined with **Esh** <note>original Hebrew: אש</note>, or **Eshto**, the **fire**, makes **Themish**, and **Themisto**, the **perfection of fire**. <note>The author is creating an etymological bridge between the Hebrew word for "complete" or "perfect" and the Greek mythological figure Themisto via the word for fire.</note>

**Thouah** <note>original Hebrew: תעה; *Ta'ah*</note>, to **wander** <note>original Latin: *vagari*</note>, to **sacrifice** <note>original Greek: θυειν, *thyein*</note>, to **kill** <note>original French: *tuer*</note>. From this comes the name **Thyaden**. 248 <note>The Thyades were the "raging" female followers of Dionysus; the author links their name to Hebrew roots for wandering or Greek roots for sacrificing/raging.</note>

# I N D E X :

->ת<- <note>The Hebrew letter Tav</note>

**Thor** or **Thurtur** <note>original Hebrew: תור</note>, **Turtledove** <note>original Dutch: *Tortelduif*</note>, from which comes **Tartarus**. 135 <note>The author suggests a linguistic connection between the Hebrew name for the turtledove and the deep abyss of Greek mythology.</note>

**Teruah** <note>original Hebrew: תרועה; transcribed in the text as *Therogne*</note>, from which comes **Triumph** <note>original Latin: *Triumphus*</note>; **wailing**, **shouting**; in later times, the **singing** and the **resounding** of assemblies. Psalm 89:16. 118 <note>The term *Teruah* refers to a trumpet blast or a collective shout of joy or alarm; the author links it to the Roman concept of a triumphal procession.</note>
